title: FAA tees up $875M AI tool to help manage air traffic congestion
gist: The FAA is launching SMART, an AI traffic-flow prediction tool from Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, at the three major Washington, DC, airports as soon as September 21 under an $875 million, 12-year contract that also replaces the Air Traffic Control System Command Center's flow management backbone. The deployment is a bet that AI can offset a controller workforce that shrank 6 percent in a decade, and the FAA has already cut its 2026-2028 controller requirement by about 2,000 people.

themes.theme: SMART contract scope and vendor economics

insights.claim: The FAA's SMART air traffic prediction tool is part of an $875 million, 12-year contract awarded in June to Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which also covers a replacement Flow Management Data and Services system for the Air Traffic Control System Command Center in Virginia.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A single private vendor now holds a 12-year, near-billion-dollar position inside US air traffic infrastructure — a durable government revenue annuity and a reference win for aviation AI.
insights.quote: SMART is part of an $875 million, 12-year contract awarded to the Boston-based company Air Space Intelligence in June.

insights.claim: Air Space Intelligence claims its separate Flyways AI platform already helps manage over 40 percent of all US air traffic through customer partnerships including Alaska Airlines, using a 4D digital twin of US national airspace.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The vendor had commercial-side airspace coverage before winning the federal contract, so the government award compounds an existing network position rather than creating one from scratch.
insights.quote: Air Space Intelligence claims its separate Flyways AI platform already helps manage over 40 percent of all US air traffic
insights.locator: Air Space Intelligence claims its separate Flyways AI platform

insights.claim: SMART's initial launch is confined to the three major airports in the Washington, DC, area as soon as Monday, September 21, as the first step toward a nationwide rollout covering the 29 million square miles of US national airspace overseen by the FAA.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A narrow pilot means the contract's full revenue and risk are back-loaded; nationwide expansion is the milestone that repriced the opportunity, not the debut.
insights.locator: An AI tool is set to start advising air traffic controllers

insights.claim: Former FAA official Philip Mann, now principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, frames the new Flow Management Data and Services system as the 'backbone' and SMART as the 'predictive layer above it,' meaning the AI product rides on a separate infrastructure replacement that must land first.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Delivery risk is sequential: delays in the unglamorous backbone replacement gate the AI layer everyone is watching.
insights.locator: In an article for Global Airspace Radar Magazine

insights.claim: It is unclear what types of AI models the FAA's SMART system uses, leaving open whether it relies on deterministic rule-following models, statistical machine learning, or generative models whose outputs can change every time and may be inaccurate.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Model class determines certification difficulty and liability exposure; opacity here is the single biggest unpriced risk in the contract.
insights.quote: It is unclear what types of AI models are being used in the new SMART system.
insights.locator: It is unclear what types of AI models

insights.claim: Philip Mann, who worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years, argues the risk in the SMART system was never any single prediction but that it is a national-scale system with AI components carrying more unknowns than anything the FAA has previously fielded, so every cut in scope shrinks the unknowns.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Reframes AI deployment risk as systemic and correlated rather than per-inference — a lens for judging every safety-critical AI rollout, not just aviation.
insights.quote: SMART’s risk was never any single prediction—it is a national-scale system with AI components carrying more unknowns than anything the FAA has fielded
insights.locator: The decision to launch SMART in a limited scope

insights.claim: Mann says the evidence he will watch before supporting the next SMART expansion is performance under real workload and degraded data rather than demonstration conditions, plus a written answer to who owns the outcome when a prediction is wrong.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Unresolved liability assignment is the practical gate on scaling safety-critical AI; watch for a published accountability framework as the real go/no-go signal.
insights.quote: What I will be watching is what evidence gates the next expansion: performance under real workload and degraded data rather than demonstration conditions, and a written answer to who owns the outcome when a prediction is wrong
insights.locator: Mann wants to know whether the SMART rollout is still limited

insights.claim: Airlines were reportedly confused for weeks about the FAA's deployment plans and only eased their concerns after the agency said SMART would not change any procedures for controllers or airlines and would instead produce 'alternative route information' delivered through existing FAA systems.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The tool was de-scoped to advisory output to win industry acquiescence, which caps its near-term efficiency benefit and therefore its measurable ROI.
insights.locator: However, the airline industry was reportedly confused for weeks

insights.claim: As described by the FAA in June, the SMART rollout is limited to aircraft flying at 24,000 feet and above, covering cruise traffic transiting that airspace plus the climbs and descents feeding the metro airports.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: An altitude floor keeps the AI out of the terminal-area regime where the fatal 2025 collision occurred, limiting both upside and blast radius for now.
insights.quote: cruise traffic transiting that airspace, plus the climbs and descents feeding the metro airports
insights.locator: Mann wants to know whether the SMART rollout is still limited

themes.theme: Controller shortage as the real driver

insights.claim: The US air traffic controller workforce has operated in what Philip Mann calls a 'permanent crisis' at minimum staffing levels ever since President Ronald Reagan fired more than 11,000 controllers in 1981.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A 45-year structural staffing deficit is what creates persistent political demand for automation spend regardless of which administration is in office.
insights.locator: The first trial run for the AI tool also comes

insights.claim: The US air traffic controller workforce declined by 6 percent over the past decade according to a Government Accountability Office report published in December 2025, with hiring and training frozen by the 2013 and 2018-2019 government shutdowns and restricted during the COVID-19 pandemic.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Headcount is shrinking while traffic is not, which makes automation procurement structurally non-discretionary — a tailwind for aviation software vendors.
insights.quote: the overall workforce declined by 6 percent over the past decade
insights.locator: Attempts to hire more air traffic controllers have fallen short

insights.claim: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy claimed 15 to 20 air traffic controllers were retiring each day during the 43-day government shutdown from October 1 to November 12, 2025, versus an average of four per day, and FAA chief Bryan Bedford described the agency as losing up to 500 controller trainees during that period.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Shutdowns are a direct, quantifiable destroyer of aviation staffing capacity — a channel through which fiscal brinkmanship transmits into operational airline risk.
insights.locator: The air traffic controller workforce was further stressed

insights.claim: In May of this year the FAA reduced the estimated number of air traffic controllers it would require for the 2026 to 2028 period by about 2,000, implying leadership is already underwriting modernization and AI tools as a substitute for headcount before SMART has flown a day of live traffic.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The agency has booked the labor savings in advance; if SMART underdelivers, the staffing gap reappears as a safety and political liability.
insights.quote: the agency reduced the estimated number of air traffic controllers it would require for the 2026 to 2028 time period by about 2,000 controllers
insights.locator: FAA leaders may be betting on the agency’s overall modernization effort

insights.claim: The FAA has just started replacing hundreds of radar systems dating back to the 1980s along with radios, telecommunication lines, and the voice switches connecting controllers to pilots, meaning the AI layer is being added on top of infrastructure that is itself mid-replacement.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A multi-billion-dollar hardware refresh running concurrently with an AI deployment multiplies integration risk and extends the spending cycle for aviation hardware suppliers.

insights.claim: On January 29, 2025, 67 people died when a US Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with an American Airlines passenger jet southeast of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, with investigators citing airport tower understaffing as one of multiple causal factors and just one controller handling both helicopter and runway traffic.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The deadliest recent US aviation accident traces to the same staffing gap SMART is meant to paper over, and it happened in the exact airspace where SMART launches first.
insights.locator: But the stakes are high as the FAA attempts to address the shortage

insights.claim: Defense of the limited-scope launch rests on the principle that narrowing deployment scope is the primary available lever for reducing unknowns in a national-scale AI system, an approach a 17-year FAA veteran called the 'right call.'
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Scope-limiting as the default AI safety control is the template regulators will likely apply to other critical-infrastructure AI, slowing but not stopping adoption.
insights.quote: Every cut in scope shrinks the unknowns.
insights.locator: The decision to launch SMART in a limited scope
